questions.q: Which metric reflects decode speed under the current batch and load conditions?
options: TTFT (time to first token)
TPOT (time per output token)
Request rate
Cold-start time
questions.explain: TPOT, or time per output token, measures how fast tokens are produced once decode is underway, reflecting decode speed under the current load.

questions.q: What is "goodput," and why do some teams track it instead of raw throughput?
options: It's identical to throughput, just a newer name
It measures only the GPU's power efficiency
It counts only the requests that also met a latency SLO, since raw throughput can hide SLO violations affecting a real share of users
It measures how many requests failed outright
questions.explain: Goodput is a stricter metric: it only counts successful throughput for requests that also met their latency target, revealing SLO violations that raw throughput numbers can mask.

questions.q: Why do serving teams typically set latency SLOs on a tail percentile like p99 rather than the average?
options: Because averages are mathematically impossible to compute for latency data
Because a good average can coexist with a meaningfully bad experience for the slowest percentage of requests, which only a tail percentile reveals
Because p99 is always a smaller number than the average
Because regulators require percentile-based reporting
questions.explain: Averages get smoothed by many fast requests even when a real share of users have a bad (slow) experience; tail percentiles like p99 reveal that worst-case experience directly.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a load-testing tool like vLLM's benchmark_serving.py or Triton's perf_analyzer?
options: To compile the model into a faster binary
To fire many concurrent requests at a serving endpoint and record per-request timing, producing realistic throughput and latency percentiles
To automatically fix slow GPU kernels
To replace the need for a tokenizer
questions.explain: Load-testing tools simulate realistic concurrent traffic against a serving endpoint, which is necessary to measure true throughput and tail latency rather than a single manual request's timing.

questions.q: In a benchmark report showing mean TTFT of 182ms and p99 TTFT of 892ms, what does the large gap between these two numbers suggest?
options: The benchmark tool is broken
Decode is unusually slow for every request
There is a meaningful tail-latency risk, likely concentrated in queuing or batch-formation delay rather than the average case
The model's output tokens are all identical
questions.explain: A wide gap between mean and p99 TTFT indicates that while most requests are fast, a tail of requests experiences much higher delay — typically from queuing or batch-formation wait, which grows nonlinearly as load increases.
